articles.title: Why do we measure root ginger in ‘thumbs’ and centimetres rather than weight? | Kitchen aide
articles.summary: When it comes to ginger, personal taste often trumps strict precision, say our experts as they get to the root of the issue. Why do so many recipes state the amount of fresh ginger in “thumbs” or centimetres. With it being so variable in shape, why don’t you use weight?
body: Cloake’s fellow columnist Georgina Hayden agrees: “Unlike measuring a ratio of risotto rice to stock, or making a cake, the typical recipes I use ginger in, such as curries, don’t have to be precise,” she says. “After all, cooking should be as instinctive as possible, rather than relying on digital scales.” However, Nick is right in that ginger does vary hugely in shape, Cloake says: “If it was a very thick piece, or it wasn’t thumb-shaped, I’d cut it so the cumulative flesh of the ginger was roughly the same as the cumulative flesh of a thumb. You’re just trying to give a rough amount, without being too prescriptive. But he’s right, we should probably move to grams.”

After all, that’s a big part of cooking, right? When Hayden writes a recipe, she says, its purpose is also to empower home cooks to take a bit of creative licence: “A knob of butter, a pinch of salt, a bunch of herbs … sometimes, vague measurements are a good thing. Also, it’s mad to get out the scales for something as small as ginger.”

articles.title: Want to know what you’re really like? Just ask the people who see you twice a year | Zoe Williams
articles.summary: Apparently, I’m the person who turns up soaking wet, sucking Haribos. Who needs lifelong friends who know you inside-out when acquaintances tell it like it is? The worst kind of professional relationship is with the person you see twice a year, in a variety of different locations, because whatever…
body: “You were really wet last time!” the photographer exclaimed, remembering our previous meeting back in March. “Well, it’s a wet country,” I replied, before the person we were there to shoot chipped in: “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” Then the photographer asked, “Have you thought about getting some wet-weather clothes, if you’re going to cycle?” and I said, “Obviously this is the first time that’s occurred to me, otherwise it would have happened at some point between March and now,” except she didn’t hear me because I had my mouth full of Haribo chewy sours.

“You ate all the Haribos last time,” my colleague observed, and I’ll skip the denials because even though I can’t remember that, it sounds true. Something about getting soaked on a bike makes me powerfully hungry – I think the sense of grievance messes with my blood sugar. “Have you ever thought of having breakfast?” came the next bolt of blue-sky thinking. It’s a great ice-breaker, making such a fist of your life choices that you become a human suggestions box, everyone mucking in with some basic improvements. But this, I insist, was two freak days of 2026; all the others have panned out fine.

articles.title: I struggled to come to terms with my mum’s death. Then I swam in the sea and suddenly felt connected to her
articles.summary: My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression. I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away. It was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey.
body: Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen. Breathing came properly. There was respite.

My swimming is far from sophisticated – my strokes are messy and I am mostly kicking from the knees. Still, I manage to move forward, albeit slowly, hugging the coastline of Turkey’s Lycian Way, turning a corner and entering an area of calm. The water is blue-green. Fish glide purposefully beneath, and I’m uplifted when I see a turtle navigating around a rock on the seabed.

I came to Turkey with SwimTrek, a Brighton-based company offering guided open-water swim tours. The plan is to complete 25km over five days. On the one hand, it is a holiday; but for me, the combination of swimming and the sea has become something more than that.

I had been feeling lost as I tried to come to terms with my mum not being here any more, and generally anxious, made worse by sleepless nights. Even on calm days, at times it felt difficult to breathe, the tightness in the throat unrelenting.
points: My mother was a keen swimmer, and she lived with depression.
I wonder if she found the same respite in the water that has helped heal me since she passed away.
It was early morning in late September, off the coast of Kaş in Turkey.
Head in the water, the knotted feeling in my throat began to loosen.

articles.title: ‘I was so sick’: is running a marathon while on a GLP-1 a bad idea?
articles.summary: As the weight-loss drugs become more common, some runners find the side-effects challenging. Here’s what experts say. Women: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed? Keri M, a marathoner in her 50s, knew the race would be terrible. This feeling couldn’t be chalked up to inexperience.
body: She ran the 2024 Philadelphia marathon fast enough to earn a coveted spot in this year’s Bank of America Chicago race, one of the eight world marathon majors.

But this half marathon felt different. It was the first time she had raced on a GLP-1. Less than a week beforehand, she had taken her first 2.5mg standard starting dose of tirzepatide, commonly sold under the names Mounjaro and Zepbound, for weight loss.
Throughout the race, Keri felt nauseous, struggling to keep down the energy gels many endurance runners rely on for fuel.
“After that half marathon, I was so sick,” she said. Keri had a “severe” reaction to the 2.5mg dose and, in hindsight, wishes that she had started at a lower dose.

articles.summary: While not exactly a fashion Garbo, Aitor Throup is difficult to pin down. After resurfacing with Umbro and Maharishi collabs earlier this year, and with a Fred Perry link-up to come in 2027, the Argentinian-British designer presents an exhibition of work on which he says he’ll build his own line…
body: Thirty years into his career Aitor Throup says he is finally ready to be a successful fashion designer. Given this revelation, “Ultra Veil,” a new exhibition of his work opening this week at the Ambika P3 (a former concrete testing facility and now exhibition space at University of Westminster in London) can be read as a statement of intent.

Who is Aitor Throup and why should you care? He’s an Argentinian-British designer who has a cultish status within streetwear, having been scouted by C.P. Company on the day he graduated from the Royal College of Art in 1996 with an unforgettable collection titled When Football Hooligans Become Hindu Gods. His graduation collection merged his experience with racism as an immigrant in England and his attraction-slash-repulsion for the dandy style of the country’s sports agitators.

articles.title: Artist Jane Benson Has Some Strong Ideas About ‘Frankenstein’
articles.summary: “Is a monster the person in society that nobody understands, and that’s why we’re afraid of it?” the artist wondered while reading Mary Shelley’s “Frankenstein.” “I’m like, That’s a woman.”
body: Popular culture would have you believe that Frankenstein, Mary Shelley’s seminal 1818 novel, is a horror story of male hubris, about a mad scientist contending with the dangers of his own creation. And it is, at least in part. But within Shelley’s critique of patriarchal power, there is another voice that is often overlooked: her own. About a third of the way into the book, the narration switches to the perspective of the so-called monster as he tells Victor Frankenstein what has happened to him during the nearly two years he and his creator have been apart.

The six chapters written in the creature’s voice contain some of the most achingly beautiful prose in the whole novel. He details how he learned to understand language and emotion. How he marveled at the warmth of the sun, the blooming of flowers, the sweetness of fruit. How he grew to love the family he tenderly observed from his hiding place, and how devastating their rejection was. He explains how he came to know anger, loneliness, loss, rage—and the vengeful acts they inspired.

articles.title: We Can’t Get Enough of All of the Art on the Spring 2027 Runways
articles.summary: Whether it's investing in a museum or inviting cultural commentators to the show, designers are embracing art more publicly than ever, and they're sharing with their audiences, too.
body: “Is fashion art?” is the perennial question in this industry. Designers are inherently creative people, who, both out of natural habit and in perpetual search for inspiration, are constantly engaging with different mediums and the cool communities that surround them. What is changing is the public prominence of these conversations, exemplified by the creators with which they partner, such as Amelia, a 32-year-old TikTok art historian and Columbia student better known as Meelz on Art, whose analysis has gotten her seated at shows by Loewe and Dior.

articles.title: The Free K-Beauty Way to Stop Hair Loss
articles.summary: According to Korean hair clinic Lee Moon Won, this habit may lead to unexpected hair shedding. Here, experts break down why that might be and offer solutions to keep hair looking full and healthy.
body: It’s the great generational debate: Side part or middle part? Where we part our hair dictates the facial features we want to play up and sets the tone for our overall vibe.

But what if this defining hair feature that we spend a lot of time contemplating comes with unexpected consequences? According to Korean hair clinic Lee Moon Won, sticking to one hair part forever might be the cause of one of our most pressing hair concerns: unwanted shedding.

There are a few reasons why this might be. Wonuk Hwang, MD, clinic director at the Cheongdam Lebelle Clinic in Seoul, explains that the exposed skin where we part our hair has less protection from environmental stressors such as the sun’s harmful UV rays, and that should always be looked at seriously. Hwang points to studies that show UV radiation can cause cellular damage to the hair follicles and scalp tissue, which could increase hair shedding after severe scalp sunburn. Even though those studies don’t mention hair parts specifically, he says that exposed scalp will always need sun protection.

body: Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

articles.title: One of the Most Unusual Jobs at Sea? Looking After 24 Cats and Dogs
articles.summary: Cunard's Queen Mary 2 is the only cruise ship in the world with a kennel on board, where pets can travel across the Atlantic with their owners.
body: This is the latest installment of our bimonthly column Crews on Cruise, spotlighting the people who work behind the scenes of the world’s most memorable voyages—from bartenders and entertainers to ship captains and expedition leaders.

Oliver Cruz has one of the more unusual jobs at sea: He is the kennel master aboard Cunard ’s Queen Mary 2, a 2,759-guest ocean liner that has been making transatlantic crossings between Southampton and New York since 2004. It is also the only cruise ship in the world to offer dedicated kennels at sea during its transatlantic voyages, with 24 spaces for dogs and cats traveling with their owners.

Cruz joined the ship in 2011, initially as a spa attendant. But when the housekeeping department learned that he had spent eight years back home in the Philippines working as a zoo guide and animal handler, with everything from snakes to crocodiles, he was moved to the kennels. He has been there ever since. “Dogs are angels,” Cruz says. “Not all angels have wings. Some of them have fur.” No surprise then that Cruz has 15 dogs of his own at home and is a member of the Philippine Animal Welfare Society.
